excerpts:
# Melting and Morphing Into Mastery: On Greg Egan’s Morphotrophic

* * *

****John Knych****

* * *

**Under Review:**  
[_Morphotrophic_](http://bookshop.org/a/79715/9781922240514) . Greg Egan. Self-published, April 2024.

* * *

Greg Egan, often considered the hardest of all hard SF authors, is mostly unknown outside of his dedicated following. No photos exist of him on the internet, he does not attend SF conventions, and he does not sign autographs. He occupies an odd place in the genre book-world in which he’s an award-winning writer, but more often awarded in translated markets than the US/UK scene.

Since 1983, Egan has published 15 novels and over 100 short stories/novellas. [_Morphotrophic_](http://bookshop.org/a/79715/9781922240514) (2024), his most recent—and self-published—novel, is a masterful step in a new direction. It’s a fascinating bio-thriller that explores themes he’s delved into throughout his career, but with a tighter narrative focus.
In _Morphotrophic_ , Egan speculates on the nature of consciousness (what would it be like to be trapped inside someone else’s mind, or to share a mind with an insect, a cat, or a lizard?), explores the ethical implications of immortality, artfully depicts the methodology of science, and investigates corporate espionage.

Egan is never explicit with his politics nor does he preach to or patronize the reader. Still, much of his work belies a deep concern for the other, no matter how different or bizarre, a critique of the powers that oppress us, and a belief that we can improve the worlds we inhabit. In a society dominated by tech titans, reprehensible politicians, increasing polarization, and immoral corporations, Egan’s novels portray indirect acts of rebellion, solidarity in the face of catastrophe, and sources of hope and inspiration.

...

She requires immediate medical attention, and is able to use cytes from her slaughtered pet pig to induce regrowth. The novel then jumps to an illegal “Swapper” meeting years later, where Ruth voluntarily attaches herself to Zaleh, another Swapper, to induce their cytes to exchange, hopefully augmenting their health and longevity. But the exchange goes wrong when Ruth’s identity copies itself and implants the copy in Zaleh’s body.

_Morphotrophic_ asks what it would mean for society, science, government, and ethics if our cells/cytes could leave us on a whim, or if we could trade our cytes with another human to improve our health or achieve immortality. Egan’s fiction excels at philosophically exploring these questions and creating a world that, once you have bought into the imaginary premise, is ruthlessly plausible, a quality of the best SF.
Egan doesn’t world-build, he world-unravels: from idioms in conversation (“it’s go immortal or go home”), to advertisements attempting to take advantage of cyte superstition, to history (generational prejudice against “Flourishers,” people with robust cytes who don’t die), to crime (“Scavengers” who steal others’ cytes), the bizarre becomes normal and the surreal becomes commonplace. Egan uses the affordance given to SF authors to stretch our imagination to create vistas of awe and revelation.

As epoch-defining technologies and systems arise in our modern world, we are forced to face new and surprising ethical dilemmas: what are the legal boundaries for gene-editing, how much should we use AI in legal procedures or education, and in what cases should we allow the implanting of neural chips? Egan’s speculative analysis of ethical dilemmas feels urgent and timely.
By grappling with these questions in fiction, in which corporate interests, scientific progress, and fallible human nature swirl and seethe, perhaps we can better grapple with our own ethical dilemmas in the real world.

Egan is a champion of the triumph of science and reason. He is also a remarkable problem-solver across a wide range of narrative challenges. He doesn’t just pose ethical questions and leave them unanswered; he also provides a blueprint for answering them and moving forward. The answers are often subtle encouragements toward empathy, trust in oneself, restraint, and patience. Once the copy of Ruth’s identity, for example, gradually becomes aware that she is in Zaleh’s mind, what should she do? First, she waits and analyzes the implications of her actions and their potential effects on Zaleh. Then she chooses the opportune moment to make herself known.

...

Egan’s emphasis during these scenes amongst scientists is always to put information in a framework, to attack an obstacle from every angle, and to problem-solve with rigor. There is a joy and validation of humanity’s scientific valor in following this investigation, and Egan’s depiction provides a window into how real progress in science occurs, throughout history and in today’s labs.

Many science fiction novels lag during the second half, as the inspiration which propelled the initial writing wanes, but in _Morphotrophic_ the pace picks up halfway through. Marla and her team are spied on by a competing research lab and infiltrated by a parasite that can hijack its host. The scene in which Marla discovers the cockroach-like parasite in Nadia’s apartment is bite-your-nails thrilling. The narrative tension never diminishes as Marla and her team hunt the parasite then communicate with it.

...

Reading Egan’s lucid prose is like traveling along the razor-sharp edge of a powerful, creative intelligence pursuing a compelling vision: tunneling through the bedrock of challenges and obstacles to achieve the glory of a breakthrough. What makes _Morphotrophic_ remarkable is also the poignant and profound ending, which lingered in me weeks after finishing the book: there is simultaneously a deep melancholy mixed with a noble embracing of a self-constructed life, marked by curiosity, empathy for the bizarre, and an insight into the absurdity of the human experience.

And one can only wait and hope, as Greg Egan continues to write and explore new fields, for whatever frontier he crosses into next.

* * *

**[John Knych](https://www.jwkash.com/)** is a professor of English at the IÉSEG School of Management in Paris. He has founded a reading community for science fiction works and has organized talks with several authors.

# Book Review: Sleep And The Soul by Greg Egan

[niklasriewald](https://niklasriewald.com/author/niklasriewald/) / [May 8, 2023](https://niklasriewald.com/2023/05/08/book-review-sleep-and-the-soul-by-greg-egan/)

Greg Egan latest short story collection “Sleep and the Soul” just dropped. It’s the kind of stories that I know and love him for, this time maybe with a touch more ambiguity and cooperation/trust as an overarching theme.

In the remainder of the blog post, I’ll give a quick rundown of the stories. If you are afraid of spoilers, don’t continue reading, but directly purchase it from one of the stores [listed here](https://www.gregegan.net/BIBLIOGRAPHY/Ebooks.html) and get into it.

The book starts with a banger. **You And Whose Army?** explores the concept of shared identity, has more than one memorable plot twist and should not miss from any “Top 5 ways in which Greg Egan villains try to cheat death” list.

...

**Night Running** is about a drug that allows you to work while sleeping. But will sleep-you always have the same priorities as awake-you?

In **Solidity** humanity has to wrestle with a calamity that is somehow reminiscent of – Stable Diffusion?

All in all I had a great time reading the short story collection. It feels very contemporary. Which is maybe not so surprising as reality seems to be catching up with Science Fiction more and more.

I’m currently reading Distress from Greg Egan which is a fun, mid-future read.
It has its pro’s and con’s, but what’s absolutely fascinating is that it reads like a checklist of obvious “hot topics” for sci fi from 2020 (RNA manipulation, viruses, gender identity and its associated politics, Siri-like intelligent agents, various others all the way to hints of how the far right, Nordic historical and yoga/ mystic types have aligned recently) - but the book was actually written over 20 years ago. It’s my first Egan novel, but there’s something Gibson-like about his prescience!
